what_it_would_take: Busy means some GPU work was running, the desktop's included, not that the GPU computes at full rate. Further fps has to come from less GPU work per frame; feeding the GPU faster has little left to give (next three rows).

area: GPU idle: the game hands work over late
what_it_would_take: Time the GPU sat idle before the game called ExecuteCommandLists for the next command buffer, mostly mid-frame (0.7-3.3 ms waits before the 5th command buffer), not at the frame start. At S15 the render thread's CPU time was about half the game's own code, 17% vkd3d and 16% NVIDIA's driver; S16 took vkd3d's locking off it. These three idle rows come from frames traced with GPU timestamps, which idle longer (4.06 ms a frame) than untraced ones, so read them as shares, not as time to win.

area: GPU idle: between the game's hand-over and vkd3d's submit
what_it_would_take: From the game's ExecuteCommandLists to vkd3d's vkQueueSubmit2. vkd3d's submission thread is busy during only about 0.15 ms of it (presenting, waiting, submitting); what holds the rest is not pinned down yet. The semaphore that orders submissions costs what a barrier would (12.5 vs 13.2 us per boundary): nothing to gain there.

area: GPU idle: submitted, GPU not started yet
unit: ms per traced frame, upper bound
what_it_would_take: Includes the 70-150 us an idle GPU takes to start a new submission, and gaps filled by command buffers recorded before the traced frame, which the timer does not see. Neither the game's nor vkd3d's CPU time.
Mostly the game's own drawing at its settings. Little room without changing what is drawn.

Five compute shaders take 5.8 ms of it. Their translation is already clean (no float-control modes, raw access chains, almost no precise math), so faster equivalents with identical output would mean rewriting the game's shaders.

Mostly particle work inside secondary command buffers, which the GPU timer files here (about 21 phase barriers a frame). S15 removed the G-buffer's transitions from UNDEFINED; the real drains left, depth layout changes (about 0.2 ms) and the present blit (0.08 ms), are inherent.

The engine demotes these on its own: in the gaming-mode launches, 506 MiB more budget during play and 532 MiB more at startup left them unchanged. They are also the least-read data per MiB (2-7 thousand accesses per MiB, against 250-860 thousand for textures in VRAM), so reading them over PCIe is what fitting the game into 3 GB costs.

area: Game over its own VRAM budget
what_it_would_take: The game decides its own usage, so there is nothing to take from vkd3d here: about 234 MiB over unpatched and 91 MiB at S12 (series v13). Its budget is the card's 3 GB minus what every process uses, so it follows the desktop: from series v16 on the desktop held about 130 MiB less, and on the same S13 build (v15 against v16) the game's budget rose from 2264 to 2396 MiB and its usage by about as much.

Within a series, S13 to S16 each moved it by 15 MiB or less; it sits about 130 MiB under S12's because the desktop has held that much less video memory since series v16 (same S13 build: 2092 to 1959 MiB). Candidates found at S12, not re-checked since: a 77 MiB scene registry mostly unused, two 64 MiB upload chunks, a 32 MiB buffer.

Done on the desktop side (gaming-mode in the dotfiles): swap-ins -73% (whole-run rates), the game's budget +506 MiB. Left with it on: about 175 MiB of non-game VRAM (Hyprland 94, the 4K console framebuffer 32, the rest not attributed to any process); each remaining piece is worth roughly 0.1-0.3% fps.
